title: The sisters' songs, three
tomorrow: a man won't let her pass on the road. what does she hand him?

lines: A FILTER THAT AGES YOUR FACE.
cards: Some photo filters will age your face by decades in a second. People laugh, or go quiet, or swipe it away fast. Ambapali did it without a filter.

In the stories she's a courtesan of Vesali, praised for her beauty, who gave her mango grove to the Buddha. In the Therigatha, she's an old nun, looking at her own body, part by part, and singing about what she sees.

teach.h: HAIR LIKE BEES, NOW LIKE BARK.
teach.b: Today's question: how do you look honestly at getting old? Ambapali's song goes verse by verse, in plain paraphrase. My hair was black as bees, curled at the tips; now it's like bark fiber.
My eyes shone like jewels; now they're dim. My teeth were like fresh buds; now they're broken. My hands were smooth; now they're like roots.
And after every verse, the same refrain: so it was, and the word of the one who speaks truth is not otherwise. No complaint. No pretending.
She agrees with what she sees. A neighbor tradition looks just as hard.

Ecclesiastes, in the Bible read by Jews and Christians, describes old age through the body too: the grinders cease because they are few, and, in the King James words, "those that look out of the windows be darkened."
Some readers hear teeth and eyes there, as in her song. That's what they share: aging read off the body, honestly, part by part.
And the honest difference: Ecclesiastes opens that chapter with "Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth," and ends with the spirit returning to God who gave it.
Ambapali's refrain turns to the Buddha's word: everything made changes, so it was.
Two old voices, facing the same mirror, each in its own words.

how: Ambapali's verses are read in Theravada teaching as a reflection on impermanence and the body; Buddhist practice includes reflecting on aging as something everyone born will meet.

o: love songs Ambapali sang when she was young and admired
poems of the early nuns, here an old nun reading her body
laments the nuns sang for their lost families

s: Ambapali's song is a lament for her lost beauty
no complaint: after every verse she agrees with what she sees. so it was.
Ecclesiastes also describes old age through the body
the grinders cease because they are few; those that look out of the windows be darkened.
Ambapali and Ecclesiastes end in the same place
Ecclesiastes turns to the Creator; Ambapali's refrain turns to the Buddha's word that all made things change.

games.q: your grandmother sighs at an old photo: 'look what happened to me.' which reply is closest to Ambapali?
o: it changed, the way everything does. you're still here looking at it.
you don't look any different at all, honestly
don't look at old photos, they only make you sad
games.why: Ambapali neither denied the change nor turned away from it. she named it, verse by verse, and said: so it was.

practice: Look at your hands for the whole sit. The lines at the knuckles, the nails, a scar, the veins. Don't judge them young or old.
Just see them as they are today, and when the bell rings, let them rest.

wordCard.voice: The sisters' songs, today Ambapali's: an old nun reading her body verse by verse, with one refrain: so it was.

orig.note: Pali name; amba is mango. She gave her mango grove to the Buddha, and later sang of her own aging.

carryVoice: So it was: she sang it to her own mirror, without flinching. Day seventeen hundred.
